doc.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002

title: Working to preserve the music and the 'not her culture' remark
summary: She resents any suggestion that jazz is not her culture, given what she endured to keep the music alive.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: this music, I was. That’s why today if it’s like the reverse prejudice now, against white musicians among some of the younger musicians coming up, some of the younger Afro- American musicians coming up, I think oh my God if you only knew how much I suffered to keep this music alive. Whether it’s singing it, spreading the word, going to the clubs, teaching it, whatever. You have no idea how hard I worked. If you know what I went through to preserve this music, it was the most important thing in my life. It came before practically anything. It was on the same level as my daughter. You would never, ever get an attitude about it’s not my culture. That was said to me one time. “Oh she’s a wonderful singer but it’s not her culture.”
I notice one of the things on your wall here, it’s a plaque from the Society of Culturally Concerned. And it says, “For lifetime achievement and major contribution to African- American music.”
